Studies of the southern flounder Paralichthys lethostigma along the southeastern United States coast have revealed pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with females substantially outpacing males in growth trajectory. In field collections spanning estuarine and nearshore habitats, the ultimate total length attained by females was found to average 91.5 cm [Li = 91.5 cm], a value that places this species among the larger paralichthyid flatfishes. By contrast, the onset of reproductive competence in females occurs at a considerably smaller size: histological analyses of ovarian tissue indicate that the total length at puberty is approximately 30 cm [Lp = approximately 30 cm], typically reached during the second or third year of life under natural thermal regimes. This delayed maturation relative to maximum size reflects a life-history strategy in which somatic growth continues well beyond the initiation of gamete production, enabling older, larger individuals to contribute disproportionately to the spawning stock. The decoupling of growth and maturation allows females to allocate resources toward body mass accumulation before investing heavily in annual reproductive bouts, a pattern consistent with iteroparous teleosts that experience size-dependent fecundity.

At the earliest life stage, newly eclosed yolk-sac larvae are minute, weighing approximately 0.00022 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00022 grams] at hatching, a mass consistent with the small pelagic eggs that characterize this genus. As larvae transition through flexion and postflexion stages to benthic juveniles, growth accelerates dramatically. By the time females recruit to the spawning population, their body mass has increased by six orders of magnitude, with wet weight at puberty estimated from length-weight relationships to be around 307 grams [Wwp = around 307 grams]. Continued somatic investment throughout adulthood pushes the asymptotic body mass of mature females to 10.7 kilograms [Wwi = 10.7 kilograms], a mass that rivals that of some congeneric species and underscores the ecological role of large female flounders as top-level benthic predators in estuarine food webs. The three-orders-of-magnitude span between birth mass and adult mass illustrates the intense selective pressure on rapid juvenile growth in habitats where predation risk is high and prey availability fluctuates seasonally.

Reproductive output in southern flounder is tightly linked to ambient temperature, a relationship that has been quantified in captive spawning trials. When maintained at a constant water temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], a regime representative of late-autumn estuarine conditions in the species' core range, gravid females exhibit a maximum annual fecundity of approximately 40,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 40,000 eggs per year]. This total is achieved through a series of partial spawnings distributed over the protracted late-fall to early-winter breeding season, a strategy that spreads reproductive effort across multiple batches and reduces the risk of complete brood loss. The dependence of egg production rate on temperature has been observed across paralichthyids, with southern flounder showing a notable sensitivity that may influence both the timing and magnitude of spawning events as coastal waters warm. Field collections of pelagic eggs confirm that the majority of annual reproductive output coincides with temperatures in the 17 to 21 °C range, suggesting fine-scale thermal cueing of vitellogenesis and spawning behavior.

The longevity of Paralichthys lethostigma, like its reproductive schedule, is strongly influenced by ambient temperature. At a sustained temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], which approximates the mean annual thermal regime experienced by populations from North Carolina to northern Florida, the maximum documented lifespan in the wild extends to 10 years [am = 10 years]. This decadal lifespan is consistent with age estimates derived from otolith increment analyses of fishery-independent survey specimens, with the oldest individuals showing distinct annuli corresponding to ten annual cycles. Senescence in older females is marked by declining fecundity and a gradual deterioration of body condition, although some individuals continue to spawn into their ninth and tenth years. The longevity of this species, combined with its iteroparous reproductive strategy and large size at maturity, positions older females as critical contributors to population resilience, particularly in heavily exploited stocks where selective removal of large individuals may truncate the age structure and reduce per-capita reproductive output.

Integrating the life-history data across southern flounder populations reveals a coherent pattern of delayed maturation and exceptionally high fecundity. The ultimate total length of 91.5 cm [Li = 91.5 cm] attained by large females is reached only after a decade of sustained growth, meaning that the most fecund individuals are also the oldest. This coupling of size and age is central to population models, because the reproductive value of a female that has survived to 10 years [am = 10 years] far exceeds that of a newly recruited spawner at a temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. At the other end of the size spectrum, the minuscule mass at hatching—0.00022 grams [Wwb = 0.00022 grams]—makes clear the vulnerability of early life stages to starvation and predation; survival through the planktonic larval phase depends on rapid first feeding and growth to a length of 30 cm [Lp = 30 cm] at puberty, when mass has already increased to approximately 307 grams [Wwp = approximately 307 grams]. Once that threshold is crossed, the onset of spawning at a temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C] can yield a remarkable annual output of 40,000 eggs per year [Ri = 40,000 eggs per year] per female. The steep scaling of fecundity with body mass, combined with the asymptotic mass of 10.7 kilograms [Wwi = 10.7 kilograms], underscores the importance of preserving the older age classes in managed fisheries.
